paras: The lynching of James Stott, James Scott and Jeff Wilson was the hanging of three men by an armed party in western Apache County, Arizona Territory, on or about August 11, 1888, after a group headed by Deputy Sheriff James D. Houck arrested them. The men were suspected of ambush shootings in the conflict between sheep and cattle raisers in the Tonto Basin, and territorial papers disagreed over whether masked men took them from the posse or the posse hanged them itself.

According to Houck, Jake Lauffer had been shot from ambush near his Pleasant Valley cabin about two weeks earlier, and the same evening two men named Cody and Coleman were fired on, and Wilson, Stott and Scott were "supposed" to have done it. The Arizona Silver Belt recalled that Stott had been discharged in 1887 after a hearing on a charge of stealing Lauffer's horse, and the Prescott Journal-Miner called his place a rendezvous for horse thieves.

The St. Johns Herald, drawing on a Wells, Fargo & Co. employee named Clymer who was at Stott's house, said Houck arrived at daylight at Stott's home on Willow Wash, covered him with a Winchester and claimed a warrant. Twenty-eight men then rode up with James Scott, who had been arrested in Pleasant Valley, and when Stott asked to see the warrant Houck said he had left it at Bear Spring. Alfred M. Ingham, an invalid boarder, later said he did not believe anyone in the party had a warrant.

In the Herald's account the party took Stott, Scott and Stott's employee Wilson toward the old Verde road and, about five miles west of Phoenix Park, "halted and hung the three." Houck's version, carried by the Arizona Champion and an Albuquerque dispatch, was that about forty masked men overpowered his posse and took the prisoners. The bodies were found hanging from trees, and the Silver Belt said they were still hanging days later, with the saddles at the foot of the tree.

The Journal-Miner reported that the county authorities were taking no action, and no report of an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage. The Herald urged that the affair be "thoroughly investigated by our authorities," noted bad blood between Stott and Houck, and the next week printed a letter blaming "personal revenge." By mid-September an administrator was to be appointed for Stott's $2,000 estate.

Nationally the story spread through a Holbrook dispatch of August 15 that called it "the murder" of the men "by outlaws" and said "unauthorized persons" had made the arrests and delivered the prisoners to "a prearranged mob of outlaws." The Sacramento Daily Record-Union had the men "lynched by cowboys," the St. Paul Daily Globe headed the item "Three of Them Hanged in Yavapi County by Outlaws," and the Hand County Press dated the hanging to "the 15th," the dispatch date. An Albuquerque dispatch ran under "Murder and the Inevitable Lynching, and More to Come," and a December year-end list named the three as "outlaws."

Arizona papers split. The Silver Belt, under "A Reign of Terror," rejected the fraudulent-warrant story and later called Stott the man "so handy with a rope and branding iron", while the Journal-Miner called Stott and Wilson "notorious characters." The St. Johns Herald in Apache County blamed "the outlaws of Pleasant Valley" for "another of their dastardly and cowardly crimes" and said it knew of no charge against Scott or Wilson.

The Herald dated Houck's arrival to "Friday morning the 10th," Ingham to the morning of August 11, and the Journal-Miner put the hanging on the afternoon of the 11th. The wire placed the hanging in Yavapai County, while the Herald put it near Phoenix Park in Apache County. The account of masked men overpowering the posse came from Houck and was repeated by the Silver Belt, while the Herald's informant, who was present at the arrest, described Houck's own party as the hangers.

accounts.label: Holbrook wire

accounts.gist: His posse captured the suspected ambushers at Stott's ranch and was overpowered by about forty masked men who took and hanged them.

accounts.gist: Houck and 28 men took Stott, Scott and Wilson without showing a warrant and themselves hanged them five miles west of Phoenix Park.

accounts.label: Eyewitness Alfred M. Ingham
accounts.gist: Twenty-eight armed men headed by Houck came before daylight on August 11; Houck said the warrants were left behind; Ingham believed there were none.

accounts.label: Journal-Miner informants
accounts.gist: Arrested on alleged fictitious charges and in charge of Houck and five others, the prisoners were taken by masked men near the Canyon Creek trail and found hanging next morning.

accounts.label: Arizona Silver Belt
accounts.gist: The fraudulent-warrant story is untrue; the men were in a deputy's custody when taken by citizens who outnumbered the posse.

framing.detail: National papers ran the Holbrook wire calling the killing 'murder' by 'outlaws' under heads like 'Three Arizona Men Lynched' and 'Three of Them Hanged in Yavapi County by Outlaws'.
The Silver Belt ('A Reign of Terror') denied the fraudulent warrant and recounted Stott's horse-theft hearing, later calling him 'so handy with a rope and branding iron'.
The Journal-Miner text (via Enterprise, 'Pleasant Valley Pastime') called Stott and Wilson 'notorious characters' and doubted the lynchers were outlaws.
The St. Johns Herald called it 'high handed', 'dastardly and cowardly', and an 'Unlawful Hanging', and demanded an investigation.
The Arizona Champion and the Albuquerque dispatch relayed Houck's account of masked men overpowering his posse.

conflicts.note: The 15th is the Holbrook dispatch date. Ingham was an eyewitness and the Enterprise is specific, so the 11th is the best-supported date for the hanging.
